structure.title: Act I · Richard teaches the audience how to watch him
structure.text: He gives us the plan for disposing of his brother, then meets that brother and speaks to him with exquisite concern. We hear both performances. Soon he attempts something so outrageous at a funeral procession that he can scarcely wait to be alone and discuss how well it went.

structure.title: Acts II–III · A private design needs public business
structure.text: A sick king wants a reconciled family. A young prince needs an escort to London. There must be meetings, decisions and people willing to announce them. Richard and Buckingham find uses for all these ordinary necessities until Londoners are asked to recognise an arrangement in whose making they had no say.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · People keep accounts
structure.text: The women Richard has passed on his way through the court can put names to what he calls political necessities. Their reckoning makes room for another London than the one he has been performing for us. As the action moves towards Bosworth, he must give orders to people whose private intentions he can no longer read.

people.name: Richard, Duke of Gloucester
people.text: Richard enjoys the interval between knowing what he will do and watching someone else discover it. His account of his own body is part of the story he tells about the man he has chosen to become. His victims have had very little say in that story.

people.name: Buckingham
people.text: Richard can talk an individual round. Buckingham helps him arrange an audience, supply a speech, and stage the public reluctance of a man who urgently wants the crown. Their association lets Shakespeare show the labour that goes into making a decision look spontaneous.

people.name: Margaret and Elizabeth
people.role: A former queen and the reigning king's wife
people.text: Margaret remembers losses from the wars that brought Edward to the throne. Elizabeth has children whose safety depends on the settlement holding. The women initially have excellent reasons to dislike each other. Listening to them together makes kinship a more exact measure of what has happened than the names of the victorious houses.

context.title: One family tree is enough to begin
context.text: Edward IV, Clarence and Richard are brothers of the house of York. Edward's children stand between Richard and the crown. Queen Elizabeth's relatives have risen with her marriage. Anyone who calls for unity in this family may have quite a definite opinion about which relatives ought to lose influence first.

notice.text: Listen to the citizens who fail to cheer.
notice.why: Buckingham has a story about the popular demand for a king. The citizens have an awkward way of standing there and giving him very little to report. That silence lets the audience measure the distance between what London wants and what can be announced in its name.

passages.quote: The citizens are mum, say not a word.

notice.why: Margaret speaks to people who believe themselves in command of the present. A line they dismiss can come back to them later in her words. Someone excluded from government has found a way of being heard in a room long after she left it.

opening: Richard tells the audience what he intends to do, then walks into the next room and tells everyone else what they need to hear. He can flatter, mourn, threaten, and pretend reluctance with astonishing speed. Watching him work is pleasurable enough to make the pleasure uncomfortable: his wit invites us into plans whose victims have no such privileged view. Shakespeare follows the making of a king through a society full of people willing to accommodate one more outrage, provided it appears to serve their interests.
